title: The Tooth Is Out. The First Move Is a Call.
subtitle: When a permanent tooth is knocked loose, one friend can contact a dentist while another protects the tooth and stays with the injured person.
imageAlt: Two friends sit together on a low wall while one makes a phone call and the other holds a small clean container.
imageConcept: A calm, unstaged scene of two friends coordinating after an accident: one calling for urgent dental advice, the other holding a small container and staying close to the injured person. No visible injury, dramatic expressions or suggestion of a guaranteed outcome.
body: Make the first minute a handoff

A tooth knocked completely out of its socket is an urgent dental injury. In the surprise of the moment, a bystander may be tempted to search online, clean up, or work out exactly what happened before asking for help. If it is clearly a permanent tooth and replantation is feasible, IADT advises attempting to put it back immediately at the scene; one friend can do this while another calls a dentist and explains what happened [1]. If replantation is not feasible, keep the tooth moist and seek immediate dental care. The International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) advises prompt care for avulsed permanent teeth; a treating dentist must assess the individual injury and decide on treatment [1]. First aid can help preserve options, but it cannot promise that a tooth will be saved.
Check what kind of tooth it is

These instructions are for a permanent, or adult, tooth—not a baby tooth. This distinction matters even when the tooth looks small or the person is young: children may already have permanent teeth, and the right response depends on which tooth was lost. If you cannot tell, say so clearly when you call and follow the dentist’s instructions rather than trying to put the tooth back. An avulsed primary tooth should not be replanted; its management is different [2]. A tooth that is chipped, pushed out of position or partly attached is also not the same as one fully knocked out. Avoid tugging on a tooth that remains in the mouth. Tell the clinician what you can see, how the injury happened and roughly when it occurred. Uncertainty is useful information, not a reason to delay the call.
Let the caller get professional direction

The caller can keep the conversation short and specific: “A permanent tooth has been knocked out. We are with the person now. What should we do, and where should we go?” Give the location, the approximate time of injury and any important details the dentist asks for. Ask whether the clinic can see the person urgently and what to do with the tooth while travelling. If the regular dentist is unavailable, ask how to reach urgent dental care locally. Keep the phone on speaker if that helps the person handling the tooth hear the advice, but do not let the call turn into a long search for the perfect service while time passes. Dental guidance treats this as urgent, and the next step is prompt professional assessment—not waiting to see whether pain or bleeding settles [3]. If there is a serious facial or jaw injury, or another immediate threat to health, follow local emergency-care guidance.
Handle the tooth by its crown

If the tooth is found, pick it up by the white part normally visible in the mouth—the crown. Avoid touching the root, the narrow part that was held in the socket. The root surface is delicate, and handling it can add damage. If the tooth is dirty, the basic aim is to remove loose debris without scrubbing or scraping it; ask the dentist on the phone what they recommend. Do not wrap it in tissue, let it sit dry on a table, or try to disinfect it with household products. The person taking care of the tooth should keep it secure and moist while the caller arranges care. MedlinePlus likewise advises handling a knocked-out tooth by the crown, not the root, and contacting a dentist right away [2]. If the tooth cannot be found, still call: absence of the tooth in hand does not make the injury less urgent.
Replanting is not a test of nerve

For a clearly permanent tooth, IADT advises attempting replantation immediately at the scene when feasible; if another person is present, they can call a dentist while you act. Replant gently and do not force the tooth; do not replant a baby tooth. If replantation is not feasible or the person is unconscious, keep the tooth moist and get immediate dental care [1]. If the person is drowsy, uncooperative or at risk of choking, do not put a tooth in their mouth. When there is doubt about the tooth type, the person’s condition or what to do, keep the tooth moist and get instructions instead. A calm helper can make this easier: explain what you are doing, ask the injured person what feels manageable, and stop if there is resistance or pain. The point is to reach professional care quickly, not to make an improvised procedure succeed.
If it cannot go back, keep it from drying

If the tooth cannot be replanted, keep it moist and take it with the injured person. Ask the dentist which storage method to use. Milk or a purpose-made tooth-preservation solution may be suitable options; do not leave the tooth dry or store it in tissue. Saliva may be mentioned in some first-aid advice, but keeping a tooth loose inside the mouth can create a choking risk, particularly for a child or anyone who is not fully alert. Do not ask someone to hold it in their cheek if they could swallow or inhale it. Cleveland Clinic’s guidance also emphasizes keeping a knocked-out tooth moist when it cannot be put back in place [3]. Let the clinician know how the tooth was stored and for how long, as well as the approximate time it left the socket. These details support assessment; they are not a reason to judge anyone’s response.
Stay with the person, not just the tooth

The injured person may be frightened, bleeding or unsure what happened. Keep them seated somewhere safe and speak plainly about the next step: “I’m calling a dentist; we’re going to follow their directions.” If there is bleeding, use clean gauze or a clean cloth as appropriate, and ask the clinician what to do. Avoid giving food or drink while you are sorting out urgent care, particularly if the person may need treatment. The friend who is not calling can gather the person’s phone, needed medication information or transport, while keeping the tooth secure. Do not drive if the driver is distressed or the person’s condition makes it unsafe. A knocked-out tooth is time-sensitive, but it is still one part of a person’s overall condition. Significant facial or jaw trauma, loss of consciousness, trouble breathing, or other serious symptoms call for local emergency services rather than a dental-only plan.
Set up a two-person plan before you need it

There is no need to stage an accident to make this easier. If you share outings with a friend, agree on a simple division of roles while you are both calm: one person calls a dentist or finds the local urgent-care route; the other stays with the injured person and handles the tooth by its crown. Save the regular dentist’s number where both people can find it, and know how you would reach urgent dental care outside office hours. Keep the key distinction in mind: these replanting instructions apply to permanent teeth, never baby teeth. If an injury happens, use the plan as a starting point, not a substitute for professional direction. Take a minute to say the steps aloud together—call, identify, handle carefully, keep moist, get care. A plan is useful when it makes the next decision clearer, while leaving room for the person’s needs and the dentist’s advice.
